title: Work, study and the ber- verbs
goal: Answer the second question every Indonesian will ask you — what you do — talk about your working day, and meet the other great prefix of the language, *ber-*.
bekal: say your job, where you work and what you study
use twenty *ber-* verbs correctly, and see the root inside each one
describe a working day from *bangun* to *pulang*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ngobrol dengan tetangga
dialogs.intro: Pak Slamet, Sarah's neighbour, has been waiting patiently for a chance to ask.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya bekerja di kantor konsultan di Kuningan.

lines.speaker: Slamet:
lines.text: Oh, jauh juga. Berangkat jam berapa?

notes: **Kerja and bekerja are the same verb.** *Kerja* is the root and the everyday form; *bekerja* is the same word wearing its *ber-* prefix, and it is what you would write. Sarah uses the full form because she is speaking to an older neighbour; Pak Slamet uses the bare root because that is normal conversation.
**Kerjanya apa? — "what is your work?"** There is that *-nya* again, doing its "the… of yours" job. Other ways to ask the same thing: *Pekerjaannya apa?*, *Kerja sebagai apa?*, or simply *Kerja apa?*

**Lho** is another particle with no dictionary meaning. It marks mild surprise or a piece of news the listener may not have realised — roughly "you know" or "actually". *Sudah bagus, lho!* is warmer than *Sudah bagus*.

**Kapan-kapan** — "some time, one of these days". Doubling *kapan* (when) makes it vague and pleasant. Indonesian does this a lot: *jalan-jalan* (wander about), *makan-makan* (have a bite together), *malu-malu* (be shy).

**Biasanya and kadang-kadang** are the two frequency words you need first: "usually" and "sometimes". They can go at the front of the sentence or straight before the verb, and both positions are correct.

grammars.title: Ber- : have, do, be in a state
body: *Ber-* is the second great prefix. Unlike *me-*, it almost never changes shape, and unlike *me-*, it survives in everyday speech.
after: Two spellings to note: *ber-* becomes **be-** before a root starting with r (*be-kerja*… actually *bekerja* comes from an old irregularity) and in *belajar*. These two are the only irregulars you will meet at A1 — learn them as words, not as rules.

*Ber-* often carries the sense of "having": *berkeluarga* (to have a family), *beristri* (to have a wife), *bermobil* (to own a car). And it is the reason *bersaudara* in Unit 7 meant "to be siblings".

grammars.title: Jobs
body: No verb needed, remember: *Saya guru* is a complete sentence.
after: Look at how many begin with **pe-**: *pengacara*, *pedagang*, *pengusaha*, *pelayan*, *petani*. That prefix means "the person who does it", built on a root: *dagang* (trade) → *pedagang* (trader), *tani* (farm) → *petani* (farmer). Spotting it turns a long unknown word into a guessable one.
To say who you work for: *Saya bekerja di…* (a place) or *Saya bekerja untuk…* (an organisation). To say your field: *Saya bekerja di bidang pendidikan* — "I work in the field of education".

sections.title: A day, from bangun to tidur

blocks.text: String these together and you can describe your whole day — which is exactly what a neighbour, a colleague or a new friend will ask you to do.

A model answer to build on: *Saya bangun jam lima, mandi, lalu sarapan. Saya berangkat jam enam dan sampai di kantor jam tujuh. Saya mulai kerja jam delapan. Makan siang jam dua belas. Saya pulang jam enam sore. Malam saya belajar bahasa Indonesia, lalu tidur jam sepuluh.*
The linking words that hold a story together: *lalu* and *kemudian* (then), *setelah itu* (after that), *sebelum* (before), *sesudah* (after), *sambil* (while doing), *akhirnya* (finally).

*Kali* means "time" in the counting sense: *sekali* (once), *dua kali* (twice), *berapa kali?* (how many times?). Do not confuse it with *waktu*, which is time in general, or *jam*, which is the clock.
